summary: Presents user requirements for SIP to support deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired people. It describes the difficulties these users face with communication tools today, and the opportunities SIP-based communication offers for text, video and other media.

plainLanguage.summary: Not everyone talks and listens the same way. This document lists what internet calling needs so people who cannot hear or speak well can use it with text and video.

questions: what does sip need for deaf users
subtitle: How SIP-based communications can support deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired individuals

tldr.problem: Deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired people face significant barriers using common communication devices and cannot easily use modern internet-based calling systems designed for voice.
tldr.mechanism: SIP can support these users by allowing flexible media streams (text, video, audio), intelligent gateways to legacy systems like textphones, and transparent transcoding services that convert between media types.
tldr.outcome: With proper SIP implementations, deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired individuals can access modern communications on equal terms, through text, video, lip-reading avatars, relay services, and other alternatives.

today: RFC 3351 is Informational and defines user requirements for SIP accessibility. These requirements have influenced SIP implementation practices, though SIP as standardized in RFC 3261 does not mandate these accessibility features—implementations must choose to support them.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
Deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired individuals currently face barriers when using common communication devices. Communication tools for these users are often primitive in design, expensive, and incompatible with modern devices. Textphones (also called TTY, TDD, or minicom) enable these users to communicate via text but often cannot interoperate with each other or with newer systems.

The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) offers potential to change this situation. SIP simplifies setting up, managing, and tearing down communication sessions between different types of devices and services. Unlike traditional voice systems, SIP can handle multiple simultaneous media streams and route them through transcoding services that convert between media types.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, deaf and hard of hearing people have trouble using modern phones because most were designed only for voice. SIP is a protocol that lets computers set up calls in flexible ways, so it could support text, video, and other options.

sections.title: Key User Requirements
sections.content:
SIP must enable connection without difficulty regardless of user abilities and preferences, supporting multiple proxies, transcoding services, and simultaneous alternative media streams. Users must be able to add or remove media streams during a call without tearing down and re-establishing the session.

SIP implementations must support user profiles that describe how a person prefers to send and receive media (text, voice, video, or combinations), which transcoding services to route media through, roaming from different devices, and anonymity to avoid discrimination. SIP should support intelligent gateways that allow existing textphone systems to connect to SIP networks. Design must be inclusive, ensuring transcoding services and user agents from different manufacturers can interoperate. Users need resource discovery and management, able to identify media stream costs and choose among transcoding services by capability and policy.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP should let you pick how you want to send and receive calls (text, video, voice, or mix them). Your preferences should follow you between devices. If you use an old textphone, there should be a gateway so it works with modern SIP systems.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Privacy
sections.content:
All third-party intermediaries and transcoding services used in sessions for deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired people must offer a confidentiality policy. Information exchanged should be secure and erased before confidentiality is breached unless otherwise required. Transcoding services must publish their confidentiality and security policies.

Users must be able to keep their abilities and preferences confidential from call recipients, avoiding possible discrimination or prejudice, while still establishing a SIP session. This is a critical requirement for equality in communications.
sections.plainLanguage: Relay services and transcoding services that help people communicate must keep everything private. A deaf person should be able to use a relay service without the person on the other end knowing unless the deaf person wants them to know.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
Several practical scenarios demonstrate SIP's potential. A relay service scenario shows a hearing person calling a household with both hearing and deaf residents. During the call, a relay service joins to transcode the hearing person's voice to text for the deaf person and speak the deaf person's typed text back to the hearing person, while voice communication between the two hearing parties continues. A media service provider scenario shows a deaf person requesting audio from a radio station as text through a transcoding service, which may fail if the service has policies against certain content types.

A sign language interface scenario has a deaf person receiving audio as XML data to operate a signing avatar while sending typed text transcoded to voice. A hard of hearing person may use lip-reading avatar software to visualize voice calls. A deaf person with a textphone can call a voice-activated menu system after a relay service joins to transcode menu prompts to text and the user's responses back to voice.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay service operator can listen to a hearing person and type what they say for a deaf person, then speak what the deaf person types. A deaf person could also see an avatar that signs, or watch a lip-reading face to understand voice calls.

sections.title: Conference Calls with Multiple Media Types
sections.content:
SIP enables complex conference calls with participants using different media. One example involves five participants: one hearing person using text, one deaf person signing, one deaf or hard of hearing person reading text and speaking, one person listening and speaking, and one person recognizing sign language and reading text. The conference server invokes transcoding services between English speech and text, English text and sign language, and sign language back to English speech, creating a chain of intermediate services.

This scenario demonstrates that SIP, combined with appropriate transcoding services and media capabilities, can support rich multi-party communication among people with diverse communication needs. Time synchronization between parallel streams, buffering of content, and coordination of real-time conversations with transcoding delays are implementation considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: In a big call with five people who communicate in different ways, SIP can chain together translation services so everyone understands everyone else. One person types, another signs, another speaks, and transcoding services convert between all these ways of talking.

sections.title: Recommendations for Developers
sections.content:
Service providers and user agent manufacturers are encouraged to prevent users from revealing their abilities and preferences publicly, offer alternative signalling methods (visual or tactile) alongside auditory alerts, and store user profiles centrally for access across devices and locations. When multiple transcoding services are available, systems should be able to select the most economical or highest quality option and display costs before a session starts.

Service providers should offer alternative streams to audio, such as text or data streams for avatars. Manufacturers of voice-activated systems are encouraged to provide visual alternatives for prompts and menus. Mobile phone manufacturers should avoid electro-magnetic interference with hearing aids. Transcoding services must keep information confidential, enable literal communication without bias, match skill-sets to user needs, behave professionally, price fairly, and continuously improve. Conference call services should help users with transcoding delays participate in real-time by identifying gaps in conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies building these systems should let people pick what information they share, offer text and visual options alongside voice, show prices upfront, and make sure relay services are professional and private.
